forecasts.label: Interest payable

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon expects to use £83m of £88m exceptional support for 2025/26, £40m to restore reserve
news_drafts.lead:
Hillingdon Council expects to use £83m of the £88m of exceptional financial support it requested for 2025/26, according to papers for the Audit, Finance & Performance Committee on 3 November. Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. Of the £83m, £40m is to restore the General Fund reserve.

The 2025/26 outturn is £7m better than the position projected in the second half of that year. The papers say this has been used to reinvest in earmarked reserves that were depleted the previous year. The 2025/26 accounts were ready for public consultation on 6 August. Government agreed amounts in principle in February 2026, before the council's budget was debated: £88m for 2025/26 and £62m for 2026/27, within £173m in principle across 2025/26 to 2027/28.

One committee paper says significant progress has been made, and also that the council "is by no means out of the woods in restoring financial stability". It says delivering this year's budget, and producing a medium-term financial strategy that reduces and eliminates dependency on the support, will be key going forward.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon reports a £50m budget gap as Cabinet is asked to consider higher fees and charges
news_drafts.lead:
Hillingdon Council has a current budget gap of £50m, according to a fees and charges report prepared for its Cabinet meeting on 22 October 2026. The report proposes increases to the charges the council makes for its services.

The report says that bringing in "some of the other increases before the end of the financial year will help the Council to reduce the reliance on Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27". Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort for councils.

The report is part of the papers for the Cabinet meeting. The extract available does not say which charges would rise, by how much, or how much each increase would raise.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon pension fund surplus hits £330m as investment returns lift funding to 124%
news_drafts.lead: Hillingdon's pension fund has swung to a surplus of £330m, up from £210m a year earlier, after delivering investment returns of 21.5% over 15 months to June. The fund's assets now cover 124% of its liabilities, up from 118%, meaning it has more than enough money to pay pensions promised to staff. The improvement means the fund needs annual investment returns of only 4.5% to stay fully funded, down from 5.1%, with a probability of 88% of achieving that target. Over five years, the fund has returned 6.7% annually, exactly matching its long-term objective, though it has underperformed its own benchmark by about 1% a year across all periods. The stronger short-term performance and improved funding position suggest recent strategy changes are beginning to take effect.

findings.headline: The Council pays £3 million annually to support individuals seeking asylum and those evicted from hotels by the Home Office
findings.detail: The paper attributes the cost to the Heathrow Airport location and to hotels commissioned by the Home Office during the pandemic. It says the Council is in discussion with the Home Office and MHCLG about the financial impact, and that the cost is not matched by additional government funding.
findings.matters: Unfunded asylum-related costs are a fixed annual pressure that the Council identifies as unique to its circumstances, which peer councils with asylum accommodation would compare against.

findings.headline: Spend on frontline services is below its comparator group, predominantly Outer London Boroughs
findings.detail: The paper says the Council continues to be well run, with spend on frontline services below its comparator group and good ratings from external oversight bodies. The paper gives no figure for the comparison.
findings.matters: A council with a deficit that also reports below-peer frontline spend shows where the pressure sits, which matters to peers comparing cost bases.
findings.figures: no figure given in the paper
findings.quote: spend on frontline services being below its comparator group (predominantly Outer London Boroughs)

findings.headline: The 2025/26 Statement of Accounts was issued on 7th August 2026, with extra resource sourced to deliver them by end of June 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement was part of the Statement of Accounts issued on 7th August 2026. Before the departmental restructure, additional resource was to be sourced so the 2025/26 accounts would be delivered by the end of June 2026 and properly quality assured.
findings.matters: The gap between the end-June target and the 7th August issue date is a timing marker for any council working to the same statutory timetable.
findings.figures: 7th August 2026 accounts issue date; end of June 2026 target
findings.quote: ensure that the 2025/26 accounts are delivered by the end of June 2026 and properly quality assured.

findings.headline: MHCLG issued Hillingdon with a Best Value Notice on 15 July 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the Notice identifies concerns about financial sustainability and resilience, financial management and governance, and organisational culture. It requires urgent action on financial sustainability, implementation of all statutory recommendations, and quarterly engagement with MHCLG. It remains in place until MHCLG confirms otherwise and is to be reviewed after 12 months.
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice is a formal government intervention with set reporting duties, and a finance director or lender would want to know its scope and review date.
findings.figures: 15 July 2026 issue date; quarterly engagement with MHCLG; review after 12 months
findings.quote: MHCLG issued the Council with a Best Value Notice on 15 July 2026:

findings.headline: Internal Audit's 2025/26 annual opinion is limited assurance, and 20% of its 24 assurance reviews gave substantial assurance
findings.detail: The paper reports 40 pieces of Internal Audit work in 2025/26, including 24 assurance reviews. Of those 24, 20% resulted in substantial assurance, 40% reasonable, 36% limited, and one no assurance. The Head of Internal Audit says a reasonable assurance opinion is achievable if the current momentum is maintained.
findings.matters: The split of assurance levels across a year's reviews is a measure of control quality that peer finance teams can compare against their own.
findings.figures: 24 assurance reviews; 20% substantial; 40% reasonable; 36% limited; one no assurance review; 40 total pieces of work
findings.quote: Of the 24 assurance reviews completed in the year, 20% resulted in a substantial assurance
